content: Stretch marks, medically referred to as striae gravidarum, develop in 50% to 90% of pregnant women. These marks initially present as red or purple streaks on the skin, which gradually fade over time, leaving pale lines. Commonly affected areas include the abdomen, breasts, and thighs. The precise cause of stretch marks remains unclear, and no topical preparation has been definitively proven to prevent their development. These marks can cause significant emotional distress for women, negatively affecting their quality of life. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of topical preparations in preventing stretch marks during pregnancy. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of October 31, 2011) and the reference lists of relevant studies. The analysis included randomized controlled trials and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared topical preparations containing active ingredients with other topical preparations, placebos (preparations without active ingredients), or no treatment at all. Three independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and quality of the trials and extracted the data. The primary outcome of interest was the presence of stretch marks, while the secondary outcome was the severity of the stretch marks. Data accuracy was verified during the analysis. Six trials involving a total of 800 women were included in the review. Of these, three trials were judged to have a low risk of bias in terms of random sequence generation, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, completeness of outcome data, and selective reporting. The results showed no statistically significant difference in the development of stretch marks between women who used topical preparations with active ingredients and those who used a placebo or received no treatment. The average risk ratio (RR) was 0.74, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) ranging from 0.53 to 1.03, based on five trials involving 474 women. A sensitivity analysis, which excluded studies with a high risk of bias, yielded similar results (average RR 0.81; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.10; four trials, 424 women). Regarding the severity of stretch marks, there was no statistically significant difference between the groups. The standardized mean difference (SMD) was -0.31, with a 95% CI ranging from -1.06 to 0.44, based on two trials involving 255 women. When comparing topical preparations with active ingredients to other topical preparations also containing active ingredients, no statistically significant difference was observed in the development of stretch marks (average RR 0.51; 95% CI 0.16 to 1.60; two trials, 305 women). Similarly, there was no significant difference in the severity of stretch marks (mean difference (MD) -0.20; 95% CI -0.53 to 0.13; one trial, 206 women). In conclusion, the review found no high-quality evidence to support the use of any topical preparation for the prevention of stretch marks during pregnancy. There is a pressing need for well-designed, methodologically rigorous randomized controlled trials with larger sample sizes to evaluate the effectiveness of these preparations. Additionally, it is essential to assess the commonly used products for preventing and treating stretch marks within the framework of robust and adequately powered trials.
